title: Districts & Gerrymandering
hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.
key_points: Many systems divide a country into districts, each electing its own representative.
How district lines are drawn affects which party wins — even with identical total votes.
Gerrymandering is drawing boundaries to favor one party or group.
Common tactics: 'packing' rivals into few districts and 'cracking' them across many to dilute their votes.
content_html: In electoral systems built on single-member districts, a country is carved into geographic constituencies, each electing one representative. That design has a quiet but powerful consequence: only who wins each district matters, not a party's nationwide vote total. So the way the boundaries are drawn can shape the result before anyone votes — the very same set of voters, grouped differently, can yield a different balance of seats.
extra_html: Gerrymandering is the deliberate exploitation of this fact: drawing district lines to favor a particular party or group. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the two classic tactics. "Packing" crowds as many of a rival's supporters as possible into a handful of districts, so they win those by lopsided margins while their votes are "wasted" everywhere else. "Cracking" does the opposite, splitting a bloc of rival voters thinly across many districts so they fall short in each one. Both let mapmakers convert a minority of votes into a majority of seats. Because the temptation is built into district-based systems, many democracies try to limit it — handing redistricting to independent commissions, requiring compact or contiguous districts, or subjecting maps to court review — though the line between legitimate boundary-drawing and manipulation is often contested.

related.hook: The same ballots can produce very different results depending on the electoral system used to count them.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

related.title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
related.hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

related.title: Racial Vote Dilution: When District Lines Split a Community
related.hook: Redrawing a map can quietly weaken a racial group's vote — split one community across enough districts and it may elect no one, even where its numbers are large.

flashcards.back_html: Drawing electoral district boundaries to favor one party or group — manipulating the map to shape the result.

flashcards.prompt: How can district lines change an outcome even with the same total votes?

choices.text: In district systems, only who wins each district counts, not the nationwide total
They change how many people are allowed to vote
They alter the order candidates appear on the ballot

flashcards.explanation_html: Because each district elects its own representative, grouping voters differently can flip which party wins more districts.

flashcards.prompt: What do the gerrymandering tactics 'packing' and 'cracking' do?

choices.text: Packing crams rivals into few districts; cracking splits them across many to dilute their votes
They both add new polling stations
They lengthen and shorten the campaign period

flashcards.explanation_html: Packing wastes a rival's votes by concentrating them; cracking spreads their supporters so thin that they win nowhere.
